output:
Sunlight looks white, but it is a mixture of every colour. Red sits at one end of that mixture, blue and violet at the other. The difference between them is wavelength: red waves are long and lazy, blue waves are short and tight.

Our air is not empty. It is packed with molecules of nitrogen and oxygen, far too small for you to see. When sunlight meets them, something uneven happens. Long red waves mostly sail past undisturbed. Short blue waves get knocked sideways and scattered in all directions across the sky.

So when you look up, away from the Sun, you are seeing blue light that has bounced around the air before reaching your eyes. The whole sky acts as the source.

Think of throwing a tennis ball and a marble through a hedge. The ball crashes straight on through, while the marble clips twigs and ricochets off at odd angles. Small things are deflected most.

Sunsets work by the same rule. Low sun means light travels through far more air, so the blue is scattered away long before it arrives. What survives the journey is red and orange.

In short, the sky is blue because air scatters short blue waves much more than long red ones.
